questions.q: What does a secure view hide that a regular view does not?
options: All numeric column values automatically
Its underlying SQL definition, from anyone except its owner
The row count returned by a query
The name of the role querying it
questions.explain: A regular view's SQL is visible via GET_DDL or SHOW VIEWS. A secure view hides that definition from everyone but its owner, useful when the query logic itself is sensitive.

questions.q: What does a row access policy control?
options: Whether a table can be dropped
Which columns exist in a table
Which rows a query returns, evaluated fresh based on the querying role
How long a query is allowed to run
questions.explain: A row access policy is a function that returns TRUE for rows a given role should see — it filters results per-query based on who's asking, not what columns exist.

questions.q: Which statement attaches an already-defined row access policy to a table?
options: CREATE VIEW ... WITH ROW POLICY
ALTER TABLE ... ADD ROW ACCESS POLICY ... ON (column)
SELECT ... APPLY POLICY
GRANT ROW POLICY TO TABLE
questions.explain: CREATE ROW ACCESS POLICY defines the filtering function; ALTER TABLE ... ADD ROW ACCESS POLICY ... ON (column) is what attaches it to a specific table's column.

questions.q: In this lesson's example, what happens when the SALES_ADMIN role and the WEST role both run SELECT * FROM transactions on the same table?
options: The query fails for any role except the table owner
WEST sees every row and SALES_ADMIN sees none
SALES_ADMIN sees every row; WEST only sees rows where region = 'WEST'
Both roles see identical results because the table has no policy
questions.explain: The row access policy function returns TRUE for SALES_ADMIN on any row, but only for rows where region_col matches CURRENT_ROLE() otherwise — so the same query returns different rows per role.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when should you reach for a secure view instead of a regular one?
options: Only when the view has zero columns
When the view's own query logic (a formula, a filter) is sensitive enough that it shouldn't be visible to everyone who can query it
Every time, since secure views always perform better
Never — secure views are deprecated in favor of row access policies
questions.explain: Secure views trade away some query-optimization shortcuts, so this lesson recommends using them specifically where hiding the definition matters, not as a default on every view.
